question: Refer to the exhibit. During a vPC peer switch reload, there is packet loss between the server and the router. Which action must be taken to prevent this behavior during future reloads?
context: Topology: two Nexus switches with OSPF uplinks on both sides, connected via vPC to a downstream server.
imageNote: Diagram: two Nexus switches each with an OSPF uplink to a router/cloud, connected to each other via vPC, both feeding a downstream server.
options: Set the routed uplink ports of the Cisco Nexus peers as orphans.
Increase the vPC delay restore timer.
Disable vPC ARP synchronize on the vPC peers.
Decrease the OSPF hello and dead interval timers.
theory: The vPC "delay restore" timer controls how long a vPC peer waits, after it comes back up, before bringing its vPC member ports back into service — this pause exists so the recovering peer's routing protocols and upstream paths have time to reconverge before traffic is sent to it again. If that timer is too short relative to how long OSPF/uplink convergence actually takes on reload, traffic destined to or from the server can be black-holed briefly; increasing delay restore gives the reloading peer enough time to be fully ready before it resumes forwarding, eliminating that packet loss on future reloads. (CCNP/CCIE DCCOR Official Cert Guide, Chapter 2 — vPC Delay Restore)
